Tepid

TEP-id -- from Latin tepidus, 'lukewarm,' rooted in tepere, 'to be warm.' · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Tepid is only slightly warm; lacking enthusiasm or energy.

Ticket sales stayed tepid throughout opening week, despite the studio's massive advertising budget.

Worked Example

Guests gave the mayor's re-election announcement a tepid round of applause that trailed off within seconds.

The applause was neither excited nor absent -- just weak and half-hearted -- which is exactly the lukewarm, unenthusiastic reaction tepid describes.

How Strong Is It? — lukewarm → tepid → unenthusiastic

lukewarm vs. tepid

lukewarm vs. tepid: His lukewarm handshake and quick exit made it clear he wasn't interested in the partnership.

unenthusiastic vs. tepid

unenthusiastic vs. tepid: Her flatly unenthusiastic 'sure, I guess' was hardly the response he'd hoped for.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — tep-

root — tep-: to be warm (Latin (tepere))

suffix — -id

suffix — -id: having the quality of (as in vivid, humid) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin tepere meant 'to be warm,' and -id means 'having the quality of,' as in vivid and humid -- so tepid is literally 'having a bit of warmth': lukewarm, and figuratively neither excited nor indifferent.

Use the root in a new word: tepidarium

Use the root in a new word: tepidarium: In an ancient Roman bathhouse, the tepidarium was the warm (but not hot) room bathers passed through on their way to the steaming caldarium.

Root Check

Word Choice

Tepid can describe literal lukewarm liquids, but it's just as often used figuratively for a weak, unenthusiastic reaction -- applause, reviews, or support that falls well short of genuine excitement.
